clue.text: Faithless son mostly purified after conversion

indicators.note: most of a word is all of it bar the last letter, which is the bit left behind here
converting something turns it into a different thing, and letters that have been converted no longer stand in the order they were given

parts.note: the word with its final letter left off
eight more letters of fodder, taken straight from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a tale of religious redemption, and both halves of it are fodder: a word docked of one letter, then a whole word, ten letters between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Faithless -> PERFIDIOUS: someone perfidious breaks the trust they were given, which is faithlessness at its most treacherous.

clue.text: Butt which smoker will use repeatedly?

definitions.meaning: in old measures a butt is a cask of ale or wine holding around a hundred gallons, nothing to do with cigarettes
the second sense is the one at the bar, refilled night after night rather than thrown away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Butt' invites the cigarette end, and that is the wrong smoking word entirely: it is the cask sense, which is why the answer is a thing you do not stub out.
explanation.definitionFit: Butt -> PIPE: both name a large cask of wine or ale; the second definition is the tobacco one, used again and again where a cigarette is used once.

clue.text: Essential queries being processed with IT

indicators.note: something still being processed has not settled into its final shape, so its letters are free to land anywhere

parts.note: seven letters of fodder
the capitals are the computing department, and both letters join the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: A helpdesk surface: queries going through IT. The capital letters look like emphasis and are really just two more letters for the pile.
explanation.definitionFit: Essential -> REQUISITE: a requisite condition is one required before anything else can follow, the same adjective sense as essential.

clue.text: That is finally lost after Roman dates?

indicators.note: what a word comes to finally is its closing letter, and that single letter is all that is taken

parts.note: the Ides were fixed days in the Roman month, the middle of March being the famous one

indicators.note: what follows after something is written behind it, so this letter joins on at the end

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.walkthrough: The clue pretends to be about something mislaid on a calendar. Latin lives on in English as the abbreviation i.e., which is what the two words shorten to.
explanation.definitionFit: That is -> ID EST: the Latin phrase abbreviated to i.e., used to introduce a restatement of what has just been said.

clue.text: Pub swinger?

parts.note: the surface sense is a person with an adventurous love life, propping up the bar
read flatly instead: the painted board hanging from a bracket over the pavement, which really does swing in the wind

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and no wordplay to take apart, so the work is choosing which sense of 'swinger' the setter means. The question mark is the nudge.
explanation.definitionFit: Pub swinger -> INN SIGN: the painted board naming a pub hangs from a bracket and swings, so the whole clue is one deadpan description of it.

clue.text: At Le Moulin Rouge, a monsieur requests reveals

indicators.note: the Moulin Rouge is a Paris cabaret, so the little words that follow are to be taken in French

parts.note: the French indefinite article
M. is how the title is abbreviated in French, as Mr is in English
to request something is to ask for it

explanation.walkthrough: A masked ball at a cabaret is the picture, and it is doing double duty: the setting is the instruction to think in French for the first two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: reveals -> UNMASKS: to unmask someone is to pull the disguise off them, revealing what the mask was there to hide.

clue.text: Psychiatrist's new, cooler chambers

indicators.note: to chamber something is to shut it in a room, so the letter beside it ends up enclosed rather than tacked on

parts.note: cooler and jug are both prison slang, so one can stand in for the other
the usual single-letter abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler chambers' reads like refrigeration and is two separate jobs: a slang word for jail, and an instruction to put something inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Psychiatrist -> JUNG: Carl Jung was a Swiss psychiatrist, so the definition names a profession and the answer is one man who practised it.

clue.text: Extreme resistance, Middle Eastern ruler barely suppresses

indicators.note: a bare thing has had its covering taken off, and here the covering is the letter at each end
to suppress a thing is to hold it down out of sight, which puts it inside what is doing the holding

parts.note: the ruler is a SULTAN, stripped of the letter at each end
R is the physicist's symbol for resistance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Extreme resistance' reads as one phrase in the surface and splits in the parse: the first word defines, the second is a single letter to be buried.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme -> ULTRA: as an adjective ultra means beyond the normal limit, the sense you hear in ultra-cautious or ultra-modern.

clue.text: Fruit company discomfiting lovers?

definitions.meaning: the sharp green fruit of a thorny garden bush, the one that goes into fools and crumbles
in British usage, to play this is to be the third person tagging along with a courting couple

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit company' looks like one phrase and a possible tech joke. Split it after the first word and both halves define the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit -> GOOSEBERRY: the green garden berry; the second definition is the idiom, where playing gooseberry means being the unwanted third with a couple.

clue.text: Hydrogen emitted originally by a pulse star?

indicators.note: a word originally is a word at its origin, meaning only the letter it starts with

parts.note: the chemical symbol
the opening letter of the word
three by four is three x four, so 'by' is the multiplication sign
taken as it stands
gram is the chickpea, one of the pulses, and a staple word in Indian cooking

explanation.walkthrough: The surface builds an astronomy picture out of five separate pieces, one of them a letter hiding as an ordinary preposition. A pulsar is the thing you are meant to see.
explanation.definitionFit: star -> HEXAGRAM: the six-pointed star made of two overlapping triangles, the shape of the Star of David.

clue.text: Nelson on track to lose Trafalgar, initially upset

indicators.note: what is lost is gone from the word altogether, not moved somewhere else in it

parts.note: Nelson Piquet won three Formula One titles, so the Nelson on a track is the Brazilian, not the admiral

indicators.note: a word taken initially gives up only the letter it begins with

parts.note: its opening letter is the one that has to go

explanation.walkthrough: Nelson and Trafalgar pull hard towards the sea battle, and that is the trap: the naval hero has nothing to do with it beyond lending his first name to a racing driver.
explanation.definitionFit: upset -> PIQUE: pique is the flare of wounded pride you feel at being slighted, as in a fit of pique.

clue.text: Second name, Brown, ridiculously pronounced

parts.note: the standard abbreviation, as on a form
umber is an earth pigment, the brown of raw and burnt umber on a paint chart

indicators.note: a word that is pronounced reaches you as a sound, so the ear rather than the page decides how the last piece is spelt

parts.note: ridiculously expensive is too expensive, so the adverb means the same as the word you say here

explanation.walkthrough: The surface hands you a former Prime Minister and a middle name, and neither is wanted: 'Brown' is a colour and the last piece is a sound, not a spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Second -> NUMBER TWO: whoever is number two in a ranking is the second one, and the phrase also names an organisation's deputy.

clue.text: Plaits braided either side of one girl's head?

definitions.text: Plaits braided either side of one girl's head

indicators.note: braiding interlaces strands so that none of them stays where it started, which is what the letters do here
the shuffled letters split into two groups and sit on both sides, leaving a gap in the middle for what follows

parts.note: six letters of fodder, counted before they are rearranged
the Roman numeral

indicators.note: the head of a word is the letter at its front, and only that letter is taken

parts.note: the letter at the front of the word

explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: read once it is a plain description of a hairstyle, read again it is fodder, a numeral and an initial with instructions on where each goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: plaits braided on either side of a girl's head are exactly what the answer names, which is why nothing is left over.

clue.text: Floor area I swept clear of corn

indicators.note: sweeping a place clear of something removes it entirely, so that letter is gone from the word it sat in

parts.note: the usual abbreviation, as in the formula for a rectangle
corn here is MAIZE, the crop, once one letter has been taken out of it
this is the letter that gets swept out, standing in the clue as an innocent pronoun

explanation.walkthrough: A farmyard surface of threshing floors and swept grain. 'Floor' is at the front doing the defining, in its knocked-flat sense rather than anything underfoot.
explanation.definitionFit: Floor -> AMAZE: to floor someone is to knock them flat, and figuratively that blow leaves them astonished.

clue.text: LA road snarled with vans from Central America

indicators.note: traffic snarled up is tangled into a knot, and tangled letters keep none of their original order

parts.note: six letters of fodder, the city abbreviated as it always is
four more letters joining the tangle

explanation.walkthrough: A Los Angeles traffic jam on the surface, and the setter has picked the one American city whose initials are also fodder. 'Snarled' does the work of both pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: from Central America -> SALVADORAN: a Salvadoran comes from El Salvador, so the answer is one Central American nationality among several.

clue.text: Article about wine circle touring grand Provençal location

indicators.note: an article written about a subject goes round it, and here the two letters do that literally, closing round everything else
to tour a place is to travel round its edges, so the piece doing the touring wraps itself round what comes next

parts.note: the indefinite article written out in full
French for wine, which the southern setting invites
the letter you draw as a ring
a grand is a thousand, and G is how the slang is written

explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions, one inside the other: the wine word opens up for a single letter, and the article closes round the lot. The surface is a wine-tasting trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Provençal location -> AVIGNON: the walled papal city on the Rhone, in Provence, so the definition names the region and the answer one place in it.

clue.text: Blast on site is most deafening

indicators.note: a blast blows a thing to pieces, and the pieces do not come down in the order they went up

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, three little words of the clue running together

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blast on site' is a building-works headline, and the first word is the instruction rather than part of it. The definition is the superlative at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: most deafening -> NOISIEST: the loudest of a group is the one whose noise comes nearest to deafening you.

clue.text: Screw up when cutting motorway reservation

indicators.note: cutting something out of a word takes it away, leaving the letters on either side to close up

parts.note: to scrumple a piece of paper is to screw it up into a crushed ball
British motorways are numbered with an M, as in the M1 and the M25, and that letter is the one cut

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has roadworks in it, which is exactly what the parse needs you to forget. The long word for crumpling is the one to find first.
explanation.definitionFit: reservation -> SCRUPLE: a scruple is the moral hesitation that holds you back, the same sense as having reservations about doing something.

clue.text: Scientists bearing crucible spill mixture

indicators.note: whatever bears a load sits underneath it, and underneath in a down entry means at the bottom of the column

parts.note: a crucible is the pot a chemist melts things in
to spill liquid is to pour it out, deliberately or not
the RI is the Royal Institution in London, the body Faraday worked at and where the Christmas Lectures are given

explanation.walkthrough: A laboratory accident on the surface, and the pieces run the other way up: the scientists are supporting the other two from below, as a down clue allows.
explanation.definitionFit: mixture -> POTPOURRI: a potpourri is a jumble of unrelated things, from the bowl of dried petals to a musical medley.

clue.text: Rival neighbours secure good survey

definitions.note: Both words are nouns for an inspection: the answer's -ing ending is a noun ending here, not the participle it looks like.

indicators.note: neighbours live side by side, so the pieces are simply set next to each other with nothing done to them

parts.note: to rival someone is to vie with them
to secure a seat or a contract is to win it
the usual one-letter abbreviation, as on a school report

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a feud over a fence, and 'neighbours' is not part of that picture at all: it is the setter telling you the pieces just sit together.
explanation.definitionFit: survey -> VIEWING: a viewing is the inspection you make of a house or an exhibit, a survey done with the eyes.

clue.text: Drive Heather around following a round or two?

definitions.note: The definition names the rounds while the answer names the activity of playing them; the question mark marks that small stretch.

parts.note: drive is the get-up-and-go that keeps someone pushing on

indicators.note: what goes around something wraps outside it, so the heather word opens in the middle to take a letter in

parts.note: ling is the heather that covers British moorland, and the capital letter makes it look like a woman
f. is the reference-book abbreviation for following, as in see page 12f.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' and 'round' both belong to the sport, which is the joke: one of them is defining and the other is a piece of the build. Heather is a plant, not a passenger.
explanation.definitionFit: a round or two -> GOLFING: a round is eighteen holes, so someone out playing one or two of them is golfing.

clue.text: Divine cleared by device that measures divinity

indicators.note: clearing a word out empties the middle of it, leaving only the letters standing at each end

parts.note: the two letters at the outside of the word, with everything between them gone
a meter is what measures a supply of gas, electricity or parking time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' and 'divinity' sit at opposite ends looking like the same idea. One is the definition; the other is just a word to be hollowed out.
explanation.definitionFit: divinity -> DEMETER: Demeter is the Greek goddess of the harvest, so the definition names the category and the answer is one deity in it.

clue.text: Chap in tights torn asunder

indicators.note: a thing torn apart comes to pieces, and the pieces cannot be relied on to lie in their old order

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the whole of the last word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Torn asunder' is a set phrase, so the two words look welded together; the setter has split them into instruction and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Chap in tights -> DANSEUR: the French word for a male ballet dancer is standard in English ballet writing, and tights are what he wears on stage.

clue.text: City trader having charcuterie delivered

indicators.note: a line delivered is a line spoken aloud, so what matters is the sound and not the spelling

parts.note: the shop that sells cold meats and cheeses is a deli, and said aloud it needs one more letter written down

explanation.walkthrough: Charcuterie makes you think of France, and the sound lands in India instead. The extra letter is silent, which is the whole of the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: City -> DELHI: the Indian capital, so the definition names the category and the answer is one particular city.

clue.text: Clubs putting on attraction that's said to be filthy

indicators.note: you put a coat on by getting inside it, so the letter ends up in the middle rather than in front

parts.note: an attraction is a lure, the thing that draws you in
C is the suit on a bridge scorecard, and the capital is there to hint at a nightclub

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an idiom rather than a synonym: the setter points at a stock phrase and lets you supply the word that always comes after the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: that's said to be filthy -> LUCRE: lucre is money, and 'filthy lucre' is very nearly the only phrase the word still turns up in.

clue.text: Turkey put aside for 50 in staff meal

indicators.note: putting one thing aside for another clears a space and says who takes it, which is a swap rather than a plain deletion

parts.note: a truncheon is the short stick a British police officer carries
TR is Turkey's international vehicle code, the pair being moved out of the way
the Roman numeral for fifty, taking the vacated place

explanation.walkthrough: A canteen surface, with the bird and the staff belonging to the same picture. Both are pulled apart: one becomes two letters of a country code, the other a police weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: meal -> LUNCHEON: the formal name for lunch, the midday meal, the word that appears on menus and invitations rather than at home.

clue.text: Pawns beginning to fall in surprise

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, and in a down entry falling means dropping to the bottom while the rest close up

parts.note: a surprise is a shock, and all five letters stay in the clue's order once the front one has moved

explanation.walkthrough: Chess pieces are the surface and no help at all. 'Pawns' is a verb here, and the wordplay is one letter taking a walk down the column.
explanation.definitionFit: Pawns -> HOCKS: to hock a watch is to pawn it, the colloquial verb behind being in hock to someone.

clue.text: Maybe decrease in tension, originally brought about

indicators.note: the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow, so nothing has to be built from synonyms
bringing a thing about turns it round to face the other way, so the run of letters is read backwards

parts.note: four consecutive letters straddle the comma, starting near the end of the first word and running into the second

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the joke: read 'decrease' as de-crease, an undoing of creases, and 'Maybe' is there to license the split. The surface is about relaxing.
explanation.definitionFit: Maybe decrease -> IRON: split the word as de-crease and it is what an iron does to a shirt, taking the creases out of it.

clue.text: Niche setter's inclined to retire?

parts.note: a niche in a wall is a recess
the setter speaks as I, so the contraction is I've with the apostrophe dropped

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' means the person who wrote the clue, one of the oldest conventions going, and it almost always turns into the single letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: inclined to retire -> RECESSIVE: a recessive gene or trait hangs back and lets the dominant one show, so it is the withdrawing one.

clue.text: Having dropped some ecstasy, calling nurse?

indicators.note: what you have dropped you no longer have, so that letter is simply gone from the word

parts.note: a calling is the career you feel drawn to follow
E is the drug's usual letter, and 'some' takes just one of the two sitting side by side

explanation.walkthrough: A hospital surface with a drug in it, and the drug is only ever one letter. The question mark admits that the definition is an example rather than a match.
explanation.definitionFit: nurse -> CARER: a carer is anyone who looks after someone unable to manage alone, and a nurse is one paid instance of that.

clue.text: Miss, once dead, oddly forgotten

indicators.note: the letters in the odd-numbered positions are the ones forgotten, so only the even ones are read

parts.note: take every second letter across the two words, counting from the second letter of the first

explanation.walkthrough: An epitaph on the surface. The comma after 'Miss' is doing a lot of work: it makes the word look like a form of address rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss -> NEED: to miss someone is to feel the want of them, which is the sense of needing them rather than failing to hit them.

clue.text: Punk gigs are about embracing singular hostility

indicators.note: punk is rotten, crumbling wood, the kind used as tinder, and something rotten has lost the shape it started with
to embrace is to take something into your arms, so the odd letter is gathered in among the rest

parts.note: seven letters of fodder in the clue's own words
a book about birds is a book on birds, so the two words swap
the grammarian's abbreviation, as in sing. and pl.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Punk gigs' reads as one phrase and is really instruction plus fodder, which is why the first word feels like scene-setting. The last word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: hostility -> AGGRESSION: both name a readiness to attack, aggression being the acting out of the feeling that hostility names.
